props.title: Useless

sections.content: **Useless (2008)** (2008) is Jia Zhangke's revealing documentary about China's fashion industry, focusing on designer Ma Ke and her anti-commercial philosophy. It's a masterful continuation of Jia's examination of modern China, following his acclaimed Still Life (2006) and 24 City (2008). The film weaves through high-end fashion houses, small-town tailors, and factory workers, creating a tapestry of China's complex relationship with clothing production and consumption. Like Wang Bing's **Tie Xi Qu: West of the Tracks** (2002), it captures industrial China's transformation with patient, observational cinematography.

sections.content: The documentary style of **Useless** (2008) builds on the observational tradition of Chinese independent cinema. Similar to Zhao Liang's **Crime and Punishment** (2007) and Wang Bing's **Bitter Money** (2016), Jia eschews traditional narration and interviews, letting images and ambient sound tell the story. His camera lingers on factory workers' hands, following their mechanical movements with the same attention he gives to haute couture fashion shows in Paris.

The film's structure mirrors works like Up the Yangtze (2007) by Yung Chang, moving between different social classes to reveal economic disparities. Jia's approach influenced later documentaries like **Cotton** (2014) by Zhou Hao and Manufactured Landscapes (2006) by Jennifer Baichwal, which similarly examine global manufacturing and its human cost. sections.content: Like Wim Wenders' **Notebook on Cities and Clothes** (1989), **Useless** transcends simple fashion documentation to become a meditation on modernity and identity. The film shares thematic DNA with **The True Cost** (2015) and **The Next Black** (2014), examining fashion's environmental and social impact. Jia's camera transforms ordinary garment workers into inadvertent performers in China's economic miracle, reminiscent of the subjects in Wang Xiaoshuai's **Beijing Bicycle** (2001).
